extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, political reformers, and general readers of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for choosing and judging forms of government (especially representative government), including social, moral, mechanical, and institutional conditions that make a polity fit for a people and conducive to social well‑being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental conditions for adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of government must be adapted to the people: (1) the people must be willing to accept it (not so repugnant as to prevent establishment); (2) they must be willing and able to keep it standing; (3) they must be willing and able to do what it requires of them (conditions of action and of self‑restraint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill illustrates each condition: repugnance can render a form impracticable (e.g., certain tribes will not submit to regular civilized government); inability or unwillingness to keep a government standing (indolence, cowardice, or being deluded) makes liberty untenable; inability to perform required forbearances or cooperate with law (perjury, shielding criminals) requires sterner powers. Failure of any condition makes a government unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of the aggregate interests of society (criterion of good government)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of a good form of government is its tendency to promote the aggregate interests of society — the whole of the interests of humanity that government can affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill stresses that government is a means; its eligibility depends on adaptation to that end. Because government can inflict great evil as well as good, evaluation must consider both direct and indirect effects on overall human well‑being and the scope government allows for attainment of social ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and Progress understood as unified test
rubrics_metrics.description: Order (preservation of existing goods) and Progress (increase/improvement) are not separate, opposing criteria; whatever promotes one tends to promote the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that agencies promoting order (e.g., police, sound finance) also promote progress by securing property, repressing crime, and freeing individuals to undertake improvement. Therefore a good government encourages those qualities that serve both permanence and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of civic virtues (industry, integrity, justice, prudence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good government fosters qualities in citizens—industry, integrity, justice, and prudence—that preserve and increase social wellbeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes these are both means of preserving existing good and of promoting improvement; policies (like fair taxation and finance) should cultivate these virtues because they sustain production, morality, and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of mental activity and originality (enterprise, courage, invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should encourage mental activity, enterprise, courage and, especially, originality/invention — qualities necessary for genuine progress and for adapting to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is required not only for creating improvements but for preserving them in changing circumstances. Governments that suppress or discourage these qualities will hinder long‑term permanence as well as progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with national habits and capacities (facilitating, not determining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should, when possible, be shaped to existing opinions, tastes, and habits, because these make acceptance and effective working easier; however, such historical basis is a facilitation, not an absolute necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill warns against sentimental elevation of 'historical basis' into a necessary condition. Where capacities are lacking, advocacy and education can prepare a people for institutions (example: Italian patriots inciting demand for freedom). Legislators should take advantage of pre‑existing habits but may also responsibly promote change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative and communicative capacity (mechanical/territorial conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical and administrative conditions — e.g., means of forming and propagating public opinion (press/newspaper), ability to collect taxes and enforce orders across territory — affect which forms of government are practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill compares the Pnyx/Forum to the press as necessary for representative government; large territories without administrative reach may break into petty principalities. Representative systems alleviate but do not wholly remove these mechanical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral integrity and engaged electorate
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative institutions require an electorate that is sufficiently interested in its government and that votes on public grounds; where electors sell votes, follow bosses, or are apathetic, representation becomes an instrument of tyranny or intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrupt or unengaged voting practices convert popular election from a check on misgovernment to an additional wheel in its machinery. Effective representation presupposes voter independence and public‑spiritedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for popular cooperation with law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A people must actively cooperate with public authorities (e.g., apprehending criminals, giving evidence) for civilized government to function with minimal coercion; where such cooperation is absent, more despotic powers may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives examples (perjury to shield criminals, bystander indifference to street violence) showing that lack of cooperation forces governments to rely on sterner repression and weakens the benefits of representative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of government’s proper sphere and the danger of meddling
rubrics_metrics.description: While the proper functions of government vary by social state, the evil a government can do is not similarly circumscribed; therefore the character of government must be judged by how its actions (and excesses) affect the whole of human interests, not only by its legitimate sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that governments may inflict any degree of harm; evaluation must attend both to what government ought to do and to what it may do wrongly. Institutional design should restrain harmful meddling while enabling needed functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit between institutional complexity and popular capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must be workable by ordinary people available to operate them; a polity should be adjusted to the knowledge, skill, and capacities of those who will have to work it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill compares choosing an instrument to choosing a constitution: even a theoretically superior form fails if the population lacks the civic capacities to operate it. This includes both cognitive and moral capacities, and practical willingness to perform civic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of social power distribution and role of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: While the distribution of material social power influences which group obtains governing authority, opinion and moral convictions are active social forces that can change political arrangements; thus the ability to shape opinion is a key factor in what government is feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues against deterministic readings of social power: influential ideas (religious or speculative) and the convictions of the instructed have produced major political changes (examples: spread of abolitionism, emancipation of serfs, Reformation), so attempts to reform institutions by educating opinion are legitimate political means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of public finance and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound systems of taxation and finance that are economical, just in distributing burdens, and do not impede industry are essential both to preserve existing prosperity and to promote further progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that good finance promotes public confidence, industry, and the moral education of the community; bad finance undermines progress and order alike. Practical arrangements should avoid unnecessarily interfering with liberty or production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical adaptability: education and advocacy to prepare for institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocating particular institutions and displaying their advantages is often necessary to educate a nation’s mind both to accept and to work the institutions when they are introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cautions reformers to be mindful of the capacities required and to avoid inciting desires too far in advance of those capacities; but also affirms that promotion of institutions is a legitimate mode of preparation (example: Italian patriots).
